c.tagline: Roman ruins, island ferries and Dalmatia's beating coastal heart.

hood_desc: The UNESCO-listed core built inside Diocletian's 4th-century Roman palace, a warren of marble lanes, the Peristyle, the cathedral bell tower and the seafront Riva promenade; the obvious first-timer base with everything on foot.
A steep, atmospheric old fishermen's quarter of narrow stone stairways climbing the slopes of Marjan just west of the palace; quiet, characterful and still within walking distance of the center.

The lively bay east of the center wrapped around Split's famous sandy Bačvice beach, home to the local picigin game, beach bars and a cluster of late-night clubs; best for sun, swimming and going out.
A leafy, upscale residential area on the wooded Marjan peninsula with the Meještrović Gallery, coastal paths and the pine-forested Marjan park; calm and green, a short walk or bus from the old town.

A compact, largely residential neighborhood just north of the palace walls near the Green Market (Pazar), with everyday shops, cafes and easy access to the bus and ferry stations; a handy, central base.

water.note: Tap water is safe and good quality throughout Croatia.

transit.hours: City buses run roughly 5:00 AM to midnight; ferries to the nearby islands follow published daily schedules, far more frequent in summer.
transit.note: Split has no metro or tram; the Promet bus network covers the city and suburbs, while Jadrolinija and other lines from the central harbor connect Split to Hvar, Brač, Šolta, Vis and beyond.
transit.pay: Buy paper bus tickets from the driver or Tisak kiosks; ferry tickets come from Jadrolinija counters and machines at the harbor. Fares are in euros and there is no single citywide smartcard.

landmarks: Diocletian's Palace
The extraordinary living heart of Split, a UNESCO-listed 4th-century Roman emperor's palace whose walls now enclose homes, bars and buzzing lanes.
Cathedral of Saint Domnius
Diocletian's mausoleum reborn as one of the world's oldest cathedrals, its Romanesque bell tower delivering superb views over the old town.
Peristyle (Peristil)
The palace's colonnaded ceremonial court, flanked by an ancient black sphinx, where visitors sip coffee on Roman steps amid street performances.
Riva Promenade
Split's palm-lined marble waterfront beneath the palace's southern wall, the city's living room for coffee, sunsets and people-watching.
Marjan Hill
A pine-covered peninsula park rising west of the old town, laced with trails, hermit chapels and lookouts over city, sea and islands.
Grgur Ninski Statue (Gregory of Nin)
Ivan Meštrović's towering bronze bishop outside the Golden Gate, whose polished big toe is rubbed daily by luck-seeking visitors.
Golden Gate (Porta Aurea)
The palace's grandest Roman gateway, once the emperor's ceremonial northern entrance, its niches and arches remarkably intact.
Ivan Meštrović Gallery
The great sculptor's seaside villa and gardens, displaying his most powerful marble and bronze works on the slopes of Marjan.
Bačvice Beach
The city's famous sandy bay minutes from the centre, birthplace of picigin, Split's beloved shallow-water ball game.
Klis Fortress
A dramatic clifftop stronghold guarding the mountain pass above Split, a Game of Thrones filming location with staggering coastal views.

train.note: Split's station sits right beside the ferry port and bus station at the south end of the harbour, a few minutes from Diocletian's Palace. Rail is the slowest way in: direct trains to Zagreb take about 6-8 hours. The only international services are seasonal summer sleepers - the Vienna train runs Wednesdays, Fridays and Sundays from 29 May to 25 September 2026, and the Budapest 'Adria' runs on alternate days from 3 July to 4 October 2026, on Tuesdays and Fridays out of Budapest in the autumn. Berths sell out in high season, so book as soon as the window opens; outside those months there is no international train at all and most travellers arrive by bus, ferry or air.

bus.note: Split Bus Station (Autobusni kolodvor, https://www.ak-split.hr/) is on the harbour front beside the ferry terminal and train station, and its site is the best place to check departures across all the operators. Coaches run down the Dalmatian coast to Dubrovnik every hour or two, taking 3h45-4h35, and inland to Zagreb in about 5 hours. International routes to Bosnia, Slovenia and Italy leave from the same terminal; carry your passport, since the Dubrovnik road still passes through the short Bosnian Neum corridor and the Sarajevo and Mostar buses cross at Kamensko. You can buy online, but tickets are also sold at the counters, and there is a small per-bag charge for luggage stowed in the hold.

ferry.note: The ferry terminal is on the main harbour, a five-minute walk from Diocletian's Palace and immediately next to the bus and train stations, so onward connections are painless. Ancona is the only international crossing: Jadrolinija sails overnight in both directions on several days a week, and in summer SNAV adds a much faster daytime service. Island sailings run all year but are far more frequent and varied between June and September, when the fast catamarans to Hvar, Korcula and Dubrovnik also operate. Car space on the Jadrolinija ferries sells out in peak weeks, so book vehicles well ahead; foot passengers can usually turn up, but not on August weekends.
